days.title: The Three-Sentence Opener
days.topic: Opening a meeting or message in three sentences instead of three paragraphs
days.objective: Open a work update in exactly three sentences: context, point, ask.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths (inhale 4s, exhale 6s). Open your mouth wide 5 times and roll your tongue around your lips 5 times each direction.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: She sells seashells by the seashore.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping S and SH crisp.

mini_lesson.title: Context, Point, Ask
mini_lesson.content: Most meetings open with too much backstory. Three sentences is enough: one for context, one for the actual point, one for what you need from the room.
key_points: Sentence 1: one line of context, nothing more
Sentence 2: your actual point, stated directly
Sentence 3: a clear ask or next step

vocabulary.meaning: giving information in a few words; brief but complete
vocabulary.example_sentence: Keep your opener concise - three sentences, no more.

vocabulary.meaning: a lengthy introduction before the main point
vocabulary.example_sentence: Cut the preamble and get straight to the ask.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Open a status update on a project you know, using exactly three sentences: context, point, ask.
speaking_prompt.tips: Count your sentences on your fingers as you speak - stop at three.

conversation.opening_question: Tight and clear. What usually tempts you to add a fourth sentence?
follow_up_questions: Who's the hardest audience to be this brief with?
What happens in meetings when openers run too long?

days.retry_instructions: If you went past three sentences, retry and cut anything that isn't context, point, or ask.

days.title: Kill "Sorry" from Every Ask
days.topic: Removing reflexive apologies from requests
days.objective: Make a direct request or ask without opening with 'sorry' or 'sorry to bother you'.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, then open and close your jaw slowly 8 times to release tension before a direct-ask drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Really lively leaders rarely ramble.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping R and L distinct, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: Why 'Sorry' Undercuts You
mini_lesson.content: Opening a reasonable request with 'sorry' signals the ask itself is a burden. Replace it with a neutral or appreciative opener that keeps your tone warm without apologizing for existing.
key_points: Swap 'Sorry to bother you, but...' for 'Quick question -' or 'Do you have a second?'
Save 'sorry' for actual mistakes, not routine requests
Gratitude works better than apology: 'Thanks in advance' instead of 'Sorry for asking'

vocabulary.meaning: done automatically, without conscious thought
vocabulary.example_sentence: Saying sorry has become a reflexive habit for many people.

vocabulary.meaning: confident and direct in stating what you want or think
vocabulary.example_sentence: An assertive request doesn't need an apology attached.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Make a work request (asking for feedback, a deadline extension, or help) in 20-25 seconds without using the word 'sorry'.
speaking_prompt.tips: If 'sorry' slips out, pause, and restate the sentence without it.

conversation.opening_question: No apology needed there, and it still sounded warm. Where do you catch yourself saying sorry the most?
follow_up_questions: Does it feel different saying the request without it?
What opener would you use instead going forward?

days.retry_instructions: If 'sorry' slipped in, retry and replace it with 'Quick question -' at the start.

days.title: Kill "I Think Maybe"
days.topic: Removing hedging language from opinions and updates
days.objective: State a work opinion or update without hedging phrases like 'I think maybe' or 'kind of'.

warmup.instructions: Say 'th-th-th' with your tongue between your teeth 10 times, then 'the-the-the' 10 times.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Thirty-three thoughtful thinkers thought through their theories.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times with visible tongue-tip placement, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: Hedging Undermines Your Point
mini_lesson.content: Phrases like 'I think maybe', 'kind of', and 'sort of' soften a statement before anyone has even pushed back. Stating the view plainly and adding nuance only if asked sounds more credible.
key_points: Replace 'I think maybe we should...' with 'I recommend...' or 'We should...'
Save hedges for genuine uncertainty, not habit
You can still invite discussion afterward: 'That's my take - what's yours?'

vocabulary.meaning: to avoid making a direct or definite statement
vocabulary.example_sentence: Try not to hedge when you already know your recommendation.

vocabulary.meaning: a firmly held belief or opinion
vocabulary.example_sentence: She stated her recommendation with real conviction.

speaking_prompt.prompt: State a recommendation or opinion on a work topic in 20-25 seconds with zero hedging words.
speaking_prompt.tips: Start with 'I recommend' or 'My view is' instead of 'I think maybe'.

conversation.opening_question: Stated with real conviction. Does removing the hedge feel riskier to you?
follow_up_questions: When is hedging actually appropriate?
Who in your life speaks with the most conviction, and what do they do differently?

days.retry_instructions: If a hedge slipped in, retry and replace it with a direct opener like 'My recommendation is...'.

days.title: Kill "Does That Make Sense?"
days.topic: Replacing self-doubting check-ins with confident closes
days.objective: End an explanation with a confident close instead of 'does that make sense?'.

warmup.instructions: Hum from your lowest comfortable note to your highest and back, 3 times, to loosen vocal range for a confident close.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Many men in many moods meet many minds.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping M and N distinct, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: Closing with Confidence, Not Doubt
mini_lesson.content: 'Does that make sense?' often signals self-doubt about your own clarity, even when the explanation was fine. A confident close invites questions without implying you weren't clear.
key_points: Replace with 'Happy to go deeper on any part of that' or 'Let me know what questions come up'
A falling, steady tone at the end signals confidence
If you genuinely want a check, ask a specific question instead: 'Which part would you like me to expand on?'

vocabulary.meaning: confident in one's own abilities or judgment
vocabulary.example_sentence: He closed the explanation in a self-assured way.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Explain a simple work process in 20 seconds, then close with a confident line instead of 'does that make sense?'.
speaking_prompt.tips: Plan your closing line before you start explaining.

conversation.opening_question: That close sounded sure of itself. What's your usual go-to closing phrase?
follow_up_questions: Does ending that way change how you feel about the explanation itself?
When would you actually want direct confirmation someone understood?

days.retry_instructions: If the old phrase slipped out, retry and swap it for 'Happy to go deeper on any part of that.'

days.title: "Tell Me About Yourself" in One Line
days.topic: Compressing your professional story into a single confident sentence
days.objective: Answer 'tell me about yourself' in one well-structured sentence, not a rambling paragraph.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths, then 5 wide jaw opens to loosen up before a tightly compressed answer.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times emphasizing each P, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: The One-Line Professional Story
mini_lesson.content: A single strong sentence - role, focus, and one standout result or interest - lands better than a two-minute history. It forces you to decide what actually matters.
key_points: Formula: '[Role] who [focuses on X], known for [one result or strength]'
Cut anything that doesn't support that one sentence
Practice it until it sounds natural, not memorized

vocabulary.meaning: to reduce something to a smaller or more essential form
vocabulary.example_sentence: Try to compress your career story into a single sentence.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Answer 'tell me about yourself' in exactly one sentence using the formula from the mini lesson.
speaking_prompt.tips: Write the sentence mentally first, then say it, don't improvise live.

conversation.opening_question: Sharp and memorable. What result or strength did you choose to highlight, and why that one?
follow_up_questions: How would this sentence change for a different audience, like a client vs. a recruiter?
What's the hardest part about cutting your story down to one line?

days.retry_instructions: If it ran past one sentence, retry and cut it down until only the essential words remain.

days.title: Problem. Solution. Ask.
days.topic: A three-part structure for raising issues at work
days.objective: Raise a work problem using the problem-solution-ask structure in under 30 seconds.

warmup.instructions: 4 diaphragmatic breaths, then say AH-EH-EE-OH-OO slowly, holding each vowel 2 seconds.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Betty bought a bit of better butter to make the batter better.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times focusing on a crisp T and D tap, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: Raising Issues Without Sounding Like a Complaint
mini_lesson.content: Naming a problem without a solution sounds like venting. Problem-solution-ask shows you've already thought it through and tells the listener exactly what you need from them.
key_points: Problem: state it factually, no blame language
Solution: your proposed fix or options
Ask: what you need from the listener - a decision, resources, or approval

vocabulary.meaning: acting in advance to deal with a problem, rather than reacting after it happens
vocabulary.example_sentence: Bringing a solution with the problem is a proactive move.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Raise a work problem you've actually faced, using problem-solution-ask, in 25-30 seconds.
speaking_prompt.tips: State the problem factually - no blame words.

conversation.opening_question: Well framed - that didn't sound like a complaint at all. How did you land on that solution?
follow_up_questions: What would you do if your proposed solution got rejected?
Is there a problem you've been avoiding raising this way?

days.retry_instructions: If the ask was missing, retry and add one final sentence stating exactly what you need.

days.title: Own the First 8 Seconds
days.topic: Strong, confident openings for any meeting
days.objective: Open a meeting or call with 8 seconds of confident, well-paced delivery before diving into content.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, 5 jaw opens, 5 lip trills, combined, to feel fully warmed up before an opening-moment drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Unique New York, unique New York, you know you need unique New York.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping every consonant distinct.

mini_lesson.title: The First 8 Seconds Set the Tone
mini_lesson.content: Listeners decide how much attention to give you in the first few seconds. A steady pace, clear first sentence, and a brief pause before continuing signals you're in control of the room.
key_points: Start with a short, complete sentence - not a trailing one
Pause briefly after your opening line before continuing
Keep your pace slightly slower than feels natural for the first sentence only

vocabulary.meaning: to hold attention and control through confident presence
vocabulary.example_sentence: A strong opener helps you command the room from second one.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Record just the opening 8-10 seconds of a meeting you'd lead - one strong sentence plus a deliberate pause.
speaking_prompt.tips: Slow your very first sentence down slightly more than feels natural.

conversation.opening_question: That opening had real presence. What usually happens in the first 10 seconds of your meetings today?
follow_up_questions: Who do you know who opens meetings particularly well?
What's one word you want people to associate with how you open a room?

days.retry_instructions: If the opener trailed off, retry and practice just that one sentence in isolation until it lands firmly.

days.title: Stop Overexplaining
days.topic: Cutting justification and padding after a decision or answer
days.objective: State a decision or answer and stop, without adding unnecessary justification afterward.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, then open your jaw wide 8 times to prepare for a deliberately short response drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Chop the chips and choose the cheapest cherries for the chutney.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping CH and J distinct from SH.

mini_lesson.title: Say It, Then Stop
mini_lesson.content: Overexplaining after a clear answer can make the answer sound less certain, as if you're convincing yourself as much as the listener. One sentence of reasoning is usually enough - then stop.
key_points: Give your answer first, reasoning second (never reasoning-only)
Limit justification to one sentence unless asked for more
Silence after your answer is fine - resist the urge to fill it

vocabulary.meaning: to explain something in excessive, unnecessary detail
vocabulary.example_sentence: Try not to overexplain a decision you're already confident about.

speaking_prompt.prompt: State a work decision (e.g. which vendor, which deadline) with exactly one sentence of reasoning, then stop.
speaking_prompt.tips: After your one reasoning sentence, consciously close your mouth and wait.

conversation.opening_question: Clean and confident - no over-justifying. Was it hard to stop yourself from adding more?
follow_up_questions: When does more explanation actually help versus hurt?
What decision do you usually over-explain the most?

days.retry_instructions: If extra justification crept in, retry and stop speaking the moment your one reasoning sentence ends.

days.title: Cut Filler Words
days.topic: Replacing 'um/uh/like' with silent pauses under work pressure
days.objective: Answer a work question for 30 seconds using a silent pause instead of a filler word when thinking.

warmup.instructions: Count slowly from 1 to 10 out loud, inserting a silent 1-second pause between each number instead of any sound.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Red leather, yellow leather, red leather, yellow leather.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping L and R distinct, then at normal speed, increasing speed each repeat.

mini_lesson.title: Pause Instead of Filler, Even Under Pressure
mini_lesson.content: Filler words spike under pressure, like being asked a surprise question in a meeting. A trained silent pause reads as composed thinking rather than as hesitation or nerves.
key_points: Notice the moment you're about to say 'um' - that's your pause cue
A 1-2 second silence feels longer to you than to the listener
Practicing counted pauses trains your brain to tolerate silence under pressure

vocabulary.meaning: calm and in control of one's emotions or reactions
vocabulary.example_sentence: She stayed composed even when put on the spot.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Answer: 'What's the status of your top priority this week?' for 30 seconds, replacing any 'um' with a silent pause.
speaking_prompt.tips: It's fine to pause - just keep it silent instead of filled.

conversation.opening_question: Good use of pauses under a put-on-the-spot question. When do filler words show up most for you at work?
follow_up_questions: What helps you feel less rushed when answering unexpectedly?
How did this feel compared to Day 1's opener drill?

days.retry_instructions: If fillers crept back in, retry at half speed first so you have time to notice and catch yourself.

days.title: Speak Under Pressure
days.topic: Staying composed when put on the spot
days.objective: Respond to a surprise, pressured question with a calm, structured answer.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths (inhale 4s, hold 4s, exhale 6s) to lower your heart rate before a pressure-style prompt.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Freshly fried fish, briskly baked bread, and sizzling spiced stew.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping every consonant distinct under the pressure of speaking continuously.

mini_lesson.title: A Script for Pressure Moments
mini_lesson.content: When caught off guard, your brain often blanks before a structure kicks in. Having one memorized formula - acknowledge, answer, offer follow-up - removes the need to improvise structure in the moment.
key_points: Acknowledge: 'Good question' or repeat part of it back
Answer: give your best current answer, even if partial
Offer follow-up: 'I can get you more detail by end of day' if needed

vocabulary.meaning: the state of being calm and in control of oneself
vocabulary.example_sentence: He kept his composure under a tough, unexpected question.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Answer this surprise question: 'Why is this project behind schedule?' using acknowledge-answer-offer, in 30-40 seconds.
speaking_prompt.tips: Don't rush - acknowledge first, then take a real breath before answering.

conversation.opening_question: Composed under pressure. What usually throws you off guard in meetings?
follow_up_questions: How do you recover when you lose your train of thought mid-answer?
What's a pressure question you wish you'd handled better in the past?

days.retry_instructions: If you froze or rushed, retry and deliberately say your acknowledgment phrase out loud before answering.

days.title: The Interview Opener
days.topic: A confident first answer in an interview setting
days.objective: Deliver a confident, structured opening answer to a common interview question.

warmup.instructions: 4 diaphragmatic breaths, then say 'sss' then 'zzz' for 5 seconds each, 3 times.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Six sticky skeletons zoomed past the sizzling zoo.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping unvoiced S distinct from voiced Z, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: Structuring Your Opening Interview Answer
mini_lesson.content: Interviewers form a strong first impression from your very first answer. A structured opener - a brief relevant fact, your current focus, and one notable result - signals confidence immediately.
key_points: Lead with a relevant fact, not a full career history
Mention what you currently focus on
Close with one notable result or strength, stated plainly

vocabulary.meaning: a close and harmonious relationship with mutual understanding
vocabulary.example_sentence: A confident opener helps build rapport right away.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Answer 'Walk me through your background' as an interview opener, in 30-40 seconds, using the structure from the mini lesson.
speaking_prompt.tips: Keep it to three parts: relevant fact, current focus, one result.

conversation.opening_question: Strong opener - confident without rambling. What result did you choose to lead with, and why?
follow_up_questions: How would this change for a different type of role?
What's the part of your background you tend to over-explain?

days.retry_instructions: If it drifted into a full history, retry and cut it back to fact-focus-result only.

days.title: Answering Hard Questions
days.topic: Responding to difficult or probing questions with composure
days.objective: Respond to a difficult question honestly and confidently, without becoming defensive.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths (inhale 4s, hold 4s, exhale 6s) to stay grounded before a difficult-question drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: The sixth sick sheik's sixth sheep's sick.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say very slowly 3 times, then gradually increase speed over 2 more repeats.

mini_lesson.title: Honest, Not Defensive
mini_lesson.content: Hard questions (about a failure, a gap, a weakness) land better when answered honestly and briefly, then redirected toward what you learned or changed - rather than over-explained or deflected.
key_points: Answer the actual question first, briefly and honestly
Add what you learned or changed as a result
Avoid deflecting onto someone else or over-justifying

vocabulary.meaning: anxious to challenge or avoid criticism
vocabulary.example_sentence: Try not to sound defensive when answering a hard question.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Answer: 'Tell me about a time you missed a deadline or made a mistake.' in 30-40 seconds, honestly and without deflecting.
speaking_prompt.tips: Say what happened in one sentence before explaining what you learned.

conversation.opening_question: Honest and composed, not defensive. How did it feel to answer that directly instead of softening it?
follow_up_questions: What question do you find hardest to answer honestly?
What changed in how you handle that situation now?

days.retry_instructions: If it sounded defensive, retry and open with a plain, factual statement of what happened.

days.title: Salary Negotiation
days.topic: Stating a number and holding your position calmly
days.objective: State a salary or rate expectation clearly and hold your position without over-justifying.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths, then plant your feet and say 'My number is...' three times in a calm, even tone.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Ninety-nine nimble numbers moved neatly in a row.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping N and M distinct, as you would stating figures.

mini_lesson.title: Stating a Number Without Flinching
mini_lesson.content: A salary number lands best stated plainly, with a brief reason, and then silence - no immediate backpedaling. Holding the pause after your number is often the hardest and most important part.
key_points: State the number directly: 'My expectation is X'
Give one brief, confident reason if needed
Stop talking after the number - let the silence sit

vocabulary.meaning: the power or advantage used to achieve a desired outcome
vocabulary.example_sentence: Your track record gives you leverage in this negotiation.

speaking_prompt.prompt: State a salary or rate expectation for a role, with one brief reason, in 20-25 seconds. End on the number, not an apology.
speaking_prompt.tips: Practice saying the number itself out loud twice before recording.

conversation.opening_question: That number held firm and didn't trail off - well done. What number would actually feel uncomfortable to say out loud?
follow_up_questions: What's your go-to reason when asked to justify your number?
How do you usually feel in the silence right after stating a number?

days.retry_instructions: If you softened the number with extra qualifiers, retry and end the sentence right after stating it.

days.title: Present to Senior Leadership
days.topic: Compressed, high-stakes updates for senior audiences
days.objective: Deliver a 45-second update suitable for a senior leadership audience: headline first, detail second.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, jaw and lip warm-ups, then review one drill from this week at normal speed.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Strong strategic stakeholders strengthen structured strategies.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping every cluster distinct.

mini_lesson.title: Headline First, Detail Second
mini_lesson.content: Senior audiences want the conclusion before the explanation. Lead with the headline (the bottom line), then give supporting detail only if there's time or if asked.
key_points: Headline: the outcome or decision in one sentence
Detail: 1-2 supporting facts, only if needed
Stop once the headline and key detail are delivered - don't pad

vocabulary.meaning: the most important factor or conclusion
vocabulary.example_sentence: Give me the bottom line before the background.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Give a 40-45 second project update as if to senior leadership, headline first, then 1-2 supporting details.
speaking_prompt.tips: Say your headline sentence before you've even planned the rest.

conversation.opening_question: Headline-first, exactly how senior leaders like it. What's your natural instinct - headline first or background first?
follow_up_questions: What detail would you cut if you only had 15 seconds?
How does this compare to your Day 1 three-sentence opener?

days.retry_instructions: If background came before the headline, retry and move your conclusion to the very first sentence.

days.title: The Boardroom Pitch
days.topic: Structuring a short, high-stakes pitch
days.objective: Deliver a 60-second boardroom-style pitch with a clear recommendation and rationale.

warmup.instructions: Stand if possible. 4 breaths, 5 shoulder rolls, 5 jaw opens, to release tension before a pitch-style drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Six slippery snails slid slowly past the sleepy seals.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping each S cluster crisp.

mini_lesson.title: Recommendation First, Rationale Second
mini_lesson.content: A boardroom pitch works best when the ask comes before the explanation. Decision-makers want to know what you're proposing immediately, then hear why.
key_points: Open with your recommendation in one sentence
Give 2 supporting reasons, each in one sentence
Close with the specific decision or approval you need

vocabulary.meaning: a set of reasons or logical basis for a course of action
vocabulary.example_sentence: Give your rationale after stating the recommendation, not before.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Pitch a recommendation (a tool, a process change, a budget request) in 50-60 seconds: recommendation first, then two reasons, then the ask.
speaking_prompt.tips: Write your one-sentence recommendation first - everything else supports it.

conversation.opening_question: Clear recommendation, right up front. What pushback do you expect in the room?
follow_up_questions: Which of your two reasons is strongest on its own?
What would you cut if you only had 20 seconds?

days.retry_instructions: If the recommendation came late, retry and move it to the very first sentence.

days.title: Handle Interruptions
days.topic: Regaining the floor calmly after being cut off
days.objective: Practice calmly reclaiming your point after a simulated interruption.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths (inhale 4s, exhale 6s), then say 'As I was saying...' in a calm, steady tone 3 times.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Freshly fried flounder flipped fast from the frying pan.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, staying calm and unrushed even as speed increases.

mini_lesson.title: Reclaiming the Floor Calmly
mini_lesson.content: Being interrupted happens in every meeting. A short bridging phrase acknowledges the interruption briefly and returns smoothly to your point without sounding flustered or defensive.
key_points: Acknowledge briefly: 'Good point -' or 'Sure -'
Bridge back: 'as I was saying...' / 'to finish that thought...'
Finish your original point before fully engaging theirs, if appropriate

vocabulary.meaning: a transitional phrase used to return to an earlier point
vocabulary.example_sentence: Use a bridge phrase to smoothly return to your point.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Start explaining a simple work point. Imagine being interrupted after one sentence, then use a bridge phrase to return and finish it. 30-40 seconds total.
speaking_prompt.tips: Say the bridge phrase out loud, even though no one actually interrupted you.

conversation.opening_question: Smooth recovery - no flustered tone at all. How do you usually feel in the moment when someone interrupts you?
follow_up_questions: Is there a situation where you tend to get interrupted the most?
What bridge phrase felt most natural to you?

days.retry_instructions: If the tone sounded flustered, retry taking one slow breath before your bridge phrase.

days.title: Say No Without Softening
days.topic: Declining a request clearly without over-apologizing
days.objective: Decline a work request clearly in one or two sentences, without excessive softening.

warmup.instructions: Say 'buh-buh-buh' 10 times with a strong lip pop on each B, then 'nuh-nuh-nuh' 10 times for a firm 'no'.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: No, not now - Ben needs a better, bigger number by noon.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping B and N crisp, then at normal speed with a firm, even tone.

mini_lesson.title: A Clear No Is a Kind No
mini_lesson.content: Over-softening a 'no' with multiple qualifiers and apologies can actually confuse the other person about whether it's really a no. A brief reason plus a clear decline is both respectful and unambiguous.
key_points: State the decline plainly: 'I'm not able to take this on right now'
Give one brief reason, not a list of excuses
Offer an alternative only if you genuinely have one

vocabulary.meaning: not open to more than one interpretation; completely clear
vocabulary.example_sentence: Make your decline unambiguous so there's no confusion later.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Decline a work request (extra task, meeting invite, favor) in one or two sentences, with one brief reason.
speaking_prompt.tips: Say the decline itself before the reason, not after.

conversation.opening_question: Clear and respectful, no over-apologizing. What requests are hardest for you to decline?
follow_up_questions: How do you usually feel right after saying no?
When is it worth offering an alternative, and when is it not?

days.retry_instructions: If it sounded over-softened, retry and state the decline as your very first sentence.

days.title: Push Back Without Aggression
days.topic: Disagreeing firmly while staying collaborative
days.objective: Push back on an idea or decision firmly, while keeping a collaborative, non-aggressive tone.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths, shoulders relaxed down, to find a firm but calm tone before a pushback drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: A big black bug bit a big black bear.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping each B crisp, then at normal speed with firm, even energy.

mini_lesson.title: Firm, Not Aggressive
mini_lesson.content: Pushing back effectively means stating your concern clearly and backing it with a reason, while keeping your tone level and inviting a response - rather than escalating volume or certainty.
key_points: State the concern plainly: 'I see this differently -'
Give one concrete reason, not emotional language
Invite response: 'What am I missing?' keeps it collaborative

vocabulary.meaning: produced or conducted by two or more parties working together
vocabulary.example_sentence: A collaborative pushback invites discussion instead of conflict.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Push back on a work decision you disagree with, in 25-35 seconds: state the concern, give a reason, invite a response.
speaking_prompt.tips: Keep your volume and pace level - don't let them rise as you disagree.

conversation.opening_question: Firm but still collaborative. How do you usually tell the difference between firm and aggressive in your own tone?
follow_up_questions: Who models this balance well that you've worked with?
What topic is hardest for you to push back on calmly?

days.retry_instructions: If tone escalated, retry keeping your volume and pace exactly the same from start to finish.

days.title: Small Talk with Executives
days.topic: Confident, concise small talk in high-status settings
days.objective: Make brief, confident small talk suitable for a conversation with a senior executive.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, then say 'why, what, where, when, which' slowly 3 times each with rounded lips on the W/WH.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Which wristwatch is a Swiss wristwatch?
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping lips rounded on W/WH sounds.

mini_lesson.title: Short, Confident, Not Over-Eager
mini_lesson.content: Small talk with senior people works best kept brief and genuine - one short observation or question, a short answer, and an easy exit - rather than over-explaining to fill the silence.
key_points: Open with a brief, specific observation or question
Answer any question they ask in one or two sentences
Let natural pauses happen - don't rush to fill them

vocabulary.meaning: graceful and composed behavior, especially in a difficult situation
vocabulary.example_sentence: She handled the small talk with real poise.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Imagine brief small talk with a senior executive in a hallway. Open with a question, then answer it yourself as if they asked you back, in 20-30 seconds.
speaking_prompt.tips: Keep your answer to two sentences max, then let the pause sit.

conversation.opening_question: Relaxed but polished. What makes executive small talk feel different from small talk with peers, for you?
follow_up_questions: What's your go-to opening line in that kind of moment?
How do you usually exit a hallway conversation gracefully?

days.retry_instructions: If the answer ran long, retry and cut it to two sentences, then stop.

days.title: Networking Openers
days.topic: Starting a professional conversation with a stranger
days.objective: Open a networking conversation with a confident, specific question or statement.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, then say 'Hi, I'm...' five times with increasing warmth and energy.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Five very fine fiddlers played five lively tunes.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times keeping F and V distinct, then at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: Specific Beats Generic
mini_lesson.content: 'How's it going?' invites a one-word answer. A specific opener tied to the event, room, or shared context gives the other person something real to respond to.
key_points: Reference something specific: the event, a speaker, a shared connection
Follow with an open question, not yes/no
Have your own one-line answer ready if they ask it back

vocabulary.meaning: truly what it is said to be; sincere
vocabulary.example_sentence: A genuine opener works better than a generic one.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Open a conversation at a networking event, referencing something specific, in 20-25 seconds, then ask an open question.
speaking_prompt.tips: Avoid 'How's it going?' - reference something specific instead.

conversation.opening_question: Specific and easy to respond to. What's the hardest part of starting a conversation at a networking event for you?
follow_up_questions: What's your go-to follow-up question once the conversation starts?
How do you usually exit a networking conversation politely?

days.retry_instructions: If the opener was generic, retry and tie it to something specific about the setting or context.

days.title: Client Conversations
days.topic: Clear, reassuring communication with clients
days.objective: Update a client on a project in a way that is clear, honest, and reassuring, even if there's a delay.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, jaw and lip warm-ups, then review one drill from this week at normal speed.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Thirty thoughtful strangers simply strolled through slippery, shimmering streets.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping every sound distinct.

mini_lesson.title: Honest and Reassuring, Not Vague
mini_lesson.content: Clients trust clear, specific updates far more than vague reassurance. State the real status, the plan, and the next check-in date - even when the news isn't perfect.
key_points: State the real status plainly, no sugar-coating
Give the concrete plan or next step
End with a specific next check-in time, not 'soon'

vocabulary.meaning: open and honest; not secretive
vocabulary.example_sentence: Being transparent about a delay builds more trust than hiding it.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Update a client on a project that's running a few days behind, in 30-40 seconds: real status, plan, next check-in date.
speaking_prompt.tips: Say the real status first - don't open with an apology.

conversation.opening_question: Honest and reassuring at the same time. What's the hardest part of delivering news like that to a client?
follow_up_questions: How do you usually decide when to check in again?
What's a client update you handled particularly well in the past?

days.retry_instructions: If the update felt vague, retry and replace any soft language ('soon', 'hopefully') with a specific date or number.

days.title: The One-Sentence Update
days.topic: Compressing a status update into a single sentence
days.objective: Give a full project status update in exactly one sentence.

warmup.instructions: 4 slow breaths, then 5 wide jaw opens to prepare for an extremely compressed answer.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, with crisp consonants.

mini_lesson.title: Status, Blocker, Next Step - in One Breath
mini_lesson.content: A truly compressed update fits status, blocker (if any), and next step into one sentence using commas or a semicolon-style pause, forcing ruthless prioritization of what matters.
key_points: Status: on track / at risk / blocked, named directly
Blocker: the one thing holding it up, if any
Next step: what happens next, in a few words

vocabulary.meaning: the current state or progress of something
vocabulary.example_sentence: Give me the status in one sentence.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Give a project status update in exactly one sentence: status, blocker (if any), next step.
speaking_prompt.tips: Draft the sentence mentally, then say it in one breath.

conversation.opening_question: Impressively compact. What did you have to cut to get it down to one sentence?
follow_up_questions: Is there a project this would be hardest to do for right now?
How does one-sentence reporting change how people listen to you?

days.retry_instructions: If it ran past one sentence, retry and cut anything that isn't status, blocker, or next step.

days.title: Speaking Up First, Not Last
days.topic: Contributing early in a discussion instead of waiting
days.objective: Practice contributing a clear point early in a discussion, as if speaking first in a meeting.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, then say 'I'd like to start by...' three times with increasing confidence.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Tom told Ted to take ten tools today.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, keeping D and T crisp at the start of words.

mini_lesson.title: Why Speaking First Matters
mini_lesson.content: Waiting to speak last often means repeating what others already said, or running out of time. Speaking early - even with a simple, honest point - signals confidence and often shapes the rest of the discussion.
key_points: Prepare one clear point before the discussion starts, not during
Use a simple opener: 'I'd like to start by...' or 'My initial take is...'
It's fine for your point to be refined later - speaking first doesn't mean speaking perfectly

vocabulary.meaning: the ability to assess and initiate things independently
vocabulary.example_sentence: Speaking up first shows initiative in a meeting.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Give your initial take on a simple work topic as if you're the first person to speak in a meeting, in 20-30 seconds.
speaking_prompt.tips: Use 'I'd like to start by...' or 'My initial take is...' as your opener.

conversation.opening_question: Confident to go first with that. What usually holds you back from speaking early in a real meeting?
follow_up_questions: How does it feel different to speak first versus last?
What's one meeting coming up where you could try this?

days.retry_instructions: If you hedged at the start, retry and open directly with 'My initial take is...'

days.title: Read the Room in 8 Seconds
days.topic: Adjusting tone and pace quickly based on the room's energy
days.objective: Practice adjusting your opening tone quickly for two different imagined room energies.

warmup.instructions: Say 'Good morning, everyone' three times - once energetic, once calm and measured, once serious.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: I did NOT say he stole the money. (Repeat, stressing a different word each time.)
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say the sentence 5 times, stressing a different word each time, noticing how meaning shifts.

mini_lesson.title: Matching Tone to the Room
mini_lesson.content: The same opening line should sound different in a high-energy kickoff versus a tense status meeting. Reading the room quickly and adjusting pace and warmth in your first sentence builds instant rapport.
key_points: High-energy room: faster pace, warmer tone, more emphasis
Tense or serious room: slower pace, steadier tone, fewer emphasized words
Decide your opening tone before you start speaking, based on the room

vocabulary.meaning: to make someone or something receptive or aware of something
vocabulary.example_sentence: Attune your opening tone to the room before you speak.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Open a meeting with 'Thanks everyone for joining' twice - once for a high-energy kickoff, once for a tense status check-in. 10-15 seconds each.
speaking_prompt.tips: Decide the room's energy in your head before each take, then let your tone follow it.

conversation.opening_question: Clearly two different rooms there. Which tone comes more naturally to you by default?
follow_up_questions: What room energy do you find hardest to read quickly?
How do you usually adjust mid-meeting if you misjudged the room?

feedback_criteria: Pace/warmth appropriate to each room type
days.retry_instructions: If the two tones sounded similar, retry exaggerating the pace and warmth difference even more.

days.title: Land a "Yes" in Three Sentences
days.topic: A compact persuasive ask using claim-benefit-ask
days.objective: Make a persuasive ask designed to get a 'yes' in exactly three sentences.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, then say 'Here's what I'm proposing...' three times with growing confidence.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Fuzzy Wuzzy was a bear, Fuzzy Wuzzy had no hair.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then with growing confidence and projection, keeping B and F distinct.

mini_lesson.title: Claim, Benefit, Ask - Three Sentences Only
mini_lesson.content: A compact persuasive pitch states what you want, why it benefits the listener, and exactly what 'yes' would mean - all in three sentences, forcing total clarity about the ask.
key_points: Sentence 1: your proposal, stated plainly
Sentence 2: the specific benefit to the listener
Sentence 3: exactly what saying yes means (the concrete ask)

vocabulary.meaning: evoking interest or attention in a powerfully irresistible way
vocabulary.example_sentence: A compelling three-sentence ask is hard to say no to.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Make a work ask (budget, headcount, a new tool) in exactly three sentences: proposal, benefit, ask.
speaking_prompt.tips: Write your three sentences mentally first - don't improvise a fourth.

conversation.opening_question: Tight and persuasive. Which of your three sentences do you think is doing the most work?
follow_up_questions: What's the most likely objection to that ask?
How would you handle it if the answer was 'let me think about it'?

days.retry_instructions: If it ran past three sentences, retry and cut anything that isn't proposal, benefit, or ask.

days.title: Handle "Send Me the Deck Offline"
days.topic: Responding gracefully when a pitch gets deferred
days.objective: Respond to a deferral ('send me the deck offline') in a way that keeps momentum rather than losing it.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths (inhale 4s, exhale 6s), then say 'Happy to follow up -' in a calm, steady tone 3 times.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Freshly fried flounder flipped fast from the frying pan.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal speed, staying calm and unrushed.

mini_lesson.title: Keeping Momentum After a Deferral
mini_lesson.content: 'Send me the deck offline' can quietly kill momentum if you just agree and move on. A brief, specific follow-up commitment keeps the conversation alive without pushing too hard in the room.
key_points: Accept the deferral gracefully, without disappointment in your tone
Name a specific next step: 'I'll send it by end of day with two key points highlighted'
Propose a specific follow-up time, not an open-ended 'let's touch base'

vocabulary.meaning: the force that keeps something moving or developing
vocabulary.example_sentence: A specific follow-up keeps the momentum from a pitch alive.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Respond to 'Great, just send me the deck offline' with a graceful accept plus a specific next step and follow-up time, in 20-30 seconds.
speaking_prompt.tips: Name an exact day/time for your follow-up, not 'soon'.

conversation.opening_question: That kept real momentum going. How do you usually feel when a pitch gets deferred like that?
follow_up_questions: What's your usual follow-up timeline in practice?
How do you decide what to highlight in a follow-up?

days.retry_instructions: If the follow-up was vague, retry and replace 'soon' with an exact day or time.

days.title: Own the Board Meeting
days.topic: Full command of a compressed, high-stakes meeting moment
days.objective: Deliver a 60-second board-meeting-style segment combining headline, rationale, and a confident close.

warmup.instructions: Stand if possible. 4 breaths, 5 shoulder rolls, jaw and lip warm-ups, to release tension before a high-stakes drill.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Strong, structured speakers strategically share thoughtful, persuasive perspectives.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly 3 times, then at normal pace, with confident projection.

mini_lesson.title: Headline, Rationale, Confident Close
mini_lesson.content: A board-level segment compresses everything practiced so far: headline first, brief rationale, and a close that states next steps plainly instead of trailing off.
key_points: Headline: your key point or recommendation in one sentence
Rationale: 1-2 sentences of supporting reasoning
Close: a clear statement of next steps, delivered with a falling, confident tone

vocabulary.meaning: the ability to project confidence and authority
vocabulary.example_sentence: A compressed, confident structure helps build command presence.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Deliver a 50-60 second board-meeting-style segment on a topic you choose: headline, rationale, confident close with next steps.
speaking_prompt.tips: Treat the close as its own sentence - plan it before you start.

conversation.opening_question: That had real command presence. Which part - headline, rationale, or close - felt strongest to you?
follow_up_questions: What would you add if you had another 30 seconds?
How does this compare to your Day 15 boardroom pitch?

days.retry_instructions: If the close trailed off, retry and practice just that final sentence alone with a firm, falling tone.

days.title: Final Pitch
days.topic: A full, polished pitch combining all 28 days of skills
days.objective: Deliver a complete 60-90 second pitch combining structure, tone, composure, and a confident close.

warmup.instructions: 4 breaths, jaw and lip warm-ups, then say Day 1's drill ('She sells seashells by the seashore') once, noticing how it feels now compared to Day 1.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers while thirty-three thoughtful strangers simply strolled through slippery, shimmering streets.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say slowly once, then at full normal speed with confident projection, as a final checkpoint.

mini_lesson.title: Bringing All 28 Days Together
mini_lesson.content: This final pitch draws on everything: a tight opener, no hedging or filler, a clear ask, composure under pressure, and a confident close. It's your certificate moment - the proof of 28 days of reps.
key_points: Open strong (Day 1, Day 7): clear first sentence, deliberate pause
Stay direct (Days 2-4, 8-9): no sorry, no hedging, no filler, no overexplaining
Close with a specific ask and a confident, falling tone (Days 6, 15, 25, 27)

vocabulary.meaning: refined and accomplished; smooth and professional in delivery
vocabulary.example_sentence: After 28 days of practice, her pitch sounds polished.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Deliver your final pitch: any work proposal or idea, 60-90 seconds, using everything practiced over the 28 days - tight opener, no hedging, clear ask, confident close.
speaking_prompt.tips: This is your certificate piece - use it to show how far you've come since Day 1.

conversation.opening_question: Congratulations on completing all 28 days - that was a genuinely polished pitch. What are you most proud of from this program?
follow_up_questions: Which single habit from these 28 days do you want to keep using every day?
How does this pitch compare to your very first recording on Day 1?

feedback_criteria: Overall clarity and pace vs Day 1
days.retry_instructions: There's no need to retry this one for perfection - if you'd like another take, just focus on sounding like yourself, at your most confident.
